[[File:A stepwise irregular graph.svg|thumb|upright=0.8|A stepwise irregular graph. The number on each vertex represents the [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] of the vertex.]]

In [[graph theory]], a '''stepwise irregular graph''' (or '''SI graph''') is a [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] in which the [[degree (graph theory)|degrees]] of any two [[adjacent (graph theory)|adjacent]] vertices differ by exactly one. This concept was introduced by [[Ivan Gutman]] in 2018 as a way to study graphs with minimal irregularity among those with non-zero edge imbalance.<ref name="Gutman2018">{{cite journal |last1=Gutman |first1=Ivan |title=Stepwise irregular graphs |journal=Applied Mathematics and Computation |volume=325 |pages=234–238 |year=2018 |doi=10.1016/j.amc.2017.12.045}}</ref>

== Definition ==
A graph <math>G = (V, E)</math> is called '''stepwise irregular''' if for every edge <math>uv \in E(G)</math>, we have <math>|d(u) - d(v)| = 1</math>, where <math>d(x)</math> denotes the [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] of vertex <math>x</math>.

More generally, a graph <math>G</math> is called a <math>k</math>-stepwise irregular graph (or <math>k</math>-SI graph) for a positive integer <math>k \ge 1</math> if <math>|d(u) - d(v)| = k</math> for every edge <math>uv \in E(G)</math>.<ref name="Alizadeh2024">{{cite arXiv |last1=Alizadeh |first1=Yaser |last2=Klavžar |first2=Sandi |last3=Langari |first3=Javaher |title=Extremal results on k-stepwise irregular graphs |year=2024 |eprint=2411.15765 |class=math.CO }}</ref> The original stepwise irregular graphs correspond to the case <math>k = 1</math>.

== Basic properties ==
Stepwise irregular graphs have several fundamental structural properties. Every stepwise irregular graph is [[bipartite graph|bipartite]]. This follows from the fact that SI graphs cannot contain [[odd cycle|odd cycles]]. In any [[cycle (graph theory)|cycle]], moving along consecutive vertices requires the degrees to alternately increase and decrease by one, which is only possible if the cycle has even length.<ref name="Gutman2018" />

Every stepwise irregular graph has an even number of edges.
This is a direct consequence of the [[Albertson index]] property and the fact that for SI graphs, the Albertson index equals the number of edges.<ref name="Gutman2018" />

In a stepwise irregular graph, every integer between the minimum degree <math>\delta(G)</math> and maximum degree <math>\Delta(G)</math> must appear as the degree of some vertex.<ref name="Bera2018">{{cite arXiv |last1=Bera |first1=Somnath |last2=Paul |first2=Prithwineel |title=Properties of stepwise irregular graphs |year=2018 |eprint=1809.03297 |class=math.CO }}</ref> The graph is naturally bipartitioned into vertices of even degree and vertices of odd degree.

== Structural results ==

=== Order constraints ===
The possible [[order (graph theory)|orders]] (number of vertices) of stepwise irregular graphs depend on their [[cyclomatic number]] <math>\gamma = m - n + 1</math>:

*[[Tree (graph theory)|Trees]] (<math>\gamma = 0</math>): The order is always odd. SI trees exist for all odd orders except 1, 5, 8, 13, and 17.<ref name="Gutman2018" />

*[[Unicyclic graph|Unicyclic graphs]] (<math>\gamma = 1</math>): The order is always even. SI unicyclic graphs exist for all even orders except 2, 4, 6, 10, and 14.<ref name="Gutman2018" />

*Bicyclic graphs (<math>\gamma = 2</math>): The order is always odd. SI bicyclic graphs exist for all odd orders except 1, 3, 7, and 11.<ref name="Gutman2018" /><ref name="Bera2018" />

*Tricyclic graphs (<math>\gamma = 3</math>): The order is always even. SI tricyclic graphs exist for all even orders except 2, 4, 6, and 8.<ref name="Bera2018" />

Connected stepwise irregular graphs exist for all orders except 1, 2, 4, and 6.<ref name="Gutman2018" /><ref name="Bera2018" />

For stepwise irregular trees with at least 1 vertex of degree <math>n</math>, the minimum order for <math>n</math> = 0, 1, 2, 3...:<ref name="Gutman2018" />

:1, 2, 3, 7, 21, 81, 391, 2283, 15657, 123301, 1096011, 10850511, 118369213... {{oeis|A392965}}

=== Diameter results ===
For <math>k</math>-stepwise irregular graphs, it has been proven that for any <math>k \ge 1</math> and any [[distance (graph theory)|diameter]] <math>d \ge 2</math>, there exists a <math>k</math>-SI graph with diameter <math>d</math>. This can be achieved using [[Graph product|graph products]] such as the [[Cartesian product of graphs|Cartesian]] and [[lexicographic product of graphs|lexicographic products]].<ref name="Alizadeh2024" />

== Extremal results ==

For a <math>k</math>-stepwise irregular graph <math>G</math> of order <math>n</math>:
:<math>\Delta(G) \le \lfloor\frac{n+k}{2}\rfloor</math>
Where <math>\Delta(G)</math> is the maximum degree of <math>G</math>. The equality holds if and only if <math>G</math> is [[isomorphism|isomorphic]] to the [[complete bipartite graph]] <math>K_{(n+k)/2, (n-k)/2}</math>.<ref name="Alizadeh2024" />

The number of edges <math>m</math> in a <math>k</math>-SI graph <math>G</math> satisfies:
:<math>m(G) \le \frac{n\Delta(G)(\Delta(G) - k)}{2\Delta(G) - k}</math>
with equality if and only if the degree complexity <math>C_d(G) = 2</math> (i.e., the graph has exactly two distinct degree values).<ref name="Alizadeh2024" />

== Graph operations ==
Stepwise irregular graphs are not [[closed set|closed]] under common [[Operation (mathematics)|graph operations]].<ref name="Bera2018" /> Removing any edge or vertex from an SI graph results in a non-SI graph. The [[Complement graph|complement]] of a [[connected graph|connected]] SI graph is never SI. The subdivision graph of an SI graph is generally not SI, except for specific cases (<math>K_2</math>, <math>K_{1,3}</math>, and [[Regular graph|3-regular graphs]]). The [[line graph]] of an SI graph is not SI, except when the original graph is [[Path graph|<math>P_4</math>]].

== Connection to graph irregularity ==
Stepwise irregular graphs are closely related to the [[Albertson index]], a measure of graph irregularity defined as:
:<math>\operatorname{Alb}(G) = \sum_{uv \in E(G)} |d(u)-d(v)|</math>
This is sometimes denoted by <math>I(G)</math> and simply called the irregularity of a graph in the literature.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Albertson |first1=M. O. |title=The irregularity of a graph |journal=Ars Combinatoria |date=1997 |volume=46 |pages=219–225 |url=https://combinatorialpress.com/article/ars/Volume%20046/volume-46-paper-16.pdf}}</ref> For stepwise irregular graphs, <math>\operatorname{Alb}(G) = m</math>, making them the least irregular graphs among those with non-zero edge imbalance.<ref name="Gutman2018" />

== Topological indices ==
The [[Wiener index]] <math>W(G)</math>, degree distance <math>DD(G)</math>, and Gutman index <math>ZZ(G)</math> of SI graphs are all even integers, as well as the first and second [[Zagreb index|Zagreb indices]] <math>M_1(G)</math> and <math>M_2(G)</math>, and the multiplicative Zagreb indices <math>\Pi_1(G)</math> and <math>\Pi_2(G)</math>.<ref name="Gutman2018" />
